cases.reply:
Both runs complete with 0 errors, and both reproduce byte-identically (the script uses a fixed seed, so these figures repeat exactly).

| Metric | No cache | `--cache` | Change |
|---|---|---|---|
| p50 | 189 ms | 129 ms | −60 ms (−31.7%) |
| p95 | 245 ms | 185 ms | −60 ms (−24.5%) |
| avg | 191.7 ms | 131.7 ms | −60.0 ms (−31.3%) |

The cache shifts every request down by a flat ~60 ms, so the absolute gain is uniform while the *relative* gain shrinks as you move up the distribution — the median nearly halves, but the tail improves less (the average tracks p50 because the shift is constant).

One caveat worth knowing before you quote these: [bench.js](bench.js) is a model, not a live measurement. Line 6 computes each latency as `(cache ? 60 : 120) + rnd()*130`, plus a fixed 300 ms stall on every 50th request. So the −60 ms is the parameter baked into the script (120→60 baseline), not an independently observed effect; and those 40 stall requests sit in the top 2%, which is why p95 still lands at 185 ms with the cache on — the fixed stall dominates the far tail, so p99 would show a much thinner gain than p50.

$ rm -rf dist && npm run build
Built dist/bundle.js from 2 files (141 bytes).   [exit 0]

## Why

[bench.js](bench.js) never measures anything. It's 13 lines that *fabricate* latencies from an arithmetic sequence:

- **Line 1** says it outright: "fixed seed, so the figures repeat."
- **Line 4–5:** a hand-rolled LCG seeded at `7`. Same seed → same numbers, every single time.

- **Nothing is concurrent.** "50 concurrent" on line 10 is a literal string. The loop is sequential and finishes in microseconds.

So the zero variance is *by construction*, not evidence of a stable system. It tells you nothing about runtime jitter, GC, contention, or network behavior.
